1:
The chapter opens on the strange difficulty of a rebuilt but half-empty capital, and the witnesses read the casting of lots as the remedy for it. The reformed John Gill fixes on the rulers, who dwelt at Jerusalem as was proper, it being the metropolis of the nation, the seat both of their offices and of the city's defence, and a standing example to draw the people to dwell there too. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lays out the whole measure: lots were cast that a tenth of the people might constantly dwell at Jerusalem and the other nine parts in the villages; for the city, though not empty, had too few inhabitants to man a wall now newly built, and Nehemiah therefore obliged one in ten of the country folk to come and dwell in it, that the population might suffice for its preservation and defence. His fellow wesleyan-arminian John Wesley adds the plain end in view, that the buildings of the city might be completed and its safety the better provided for.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the reluctance itself into a mirror of the heart. Jerusalem is called the holy city, he says, because there stood the temple and the place God had chosen to put his name; one would think the holy seed would have striven for a habitation there, yet they declined it. He finds three causes: a stricter conversation was expected of its dwellers than many would come up to, so that those who care not to be holy are shy of a holy city; it was, of all places, the most hated by the heathen and the very post of danger, and fear of trouble keeps many out of the holy city; and it was more for their worldly advantage to dwell in the country, Jerusalem being no trading city where money might be got. Note, he adds, all seek their own, and not the things that are Jesus Christ's (Phil. 2:21).

By what means, then, was the city replenished? Henry answers with the same three that fill the verse: the rulers dwelt there, for there were set the thrones of judgment (Ps. 122:5), and their example brought holiness into reputation, for the mighty are magnetic; some willingly offered themselves, foregoing their own interest for the public good; and the rest were brought in by lot, in the proportion of one in ten, the disposal whereof all knew was of the Lord, so ordered to prevent strife and to answer the ancient rule of giving the tenth to God. Those shall prosper, Henry closes, that thus love Zion (Ps. 122:6); and what is given to the holy city, God reckons given to himself.
2:
The volunteers who chose Jerusalem freely are singled out for the people's blessing, and the witnesses dwell on both the gift and the gratitude. The reformed John Gill marks the difference these free settlers make to the register: the people blessed all the men that willingly offered themselves, not those taken by lot but those who of their own accord settled in the city; and it is this that distinguishes the fuller list here from a barer one elsewhere, for this takes in all who settled there, whether by choice or by lot. They were praised, he says, and men wished them all happiness and prosperity, since they denied themselves ease and profit for the public good.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads their choice as a costly one. Some volunteered their services, which was accounted a sacrifice to patriotism in that day, for Jerusalem then afforded few advantages and was a place of no small danger; hence the people spoke well of them, and, he doubts not, prayed God's blessing upon them. His fellow wesleyan-arminian John Wesley presses the same point of self-denial: they were blessed because they gave up their own safety and profit for the public good, this city being the very butt of all the malicious plots of their enemies, and for the present rather chargeable to its inhabitants than beneficial.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, whose eye is on the register that now begins, take the following title as the key to the whole: these are the heads of the province who dwelt at Jerusalem, while in the cities of Judah dwelt every one in his possession. The word rendered province, they explain, is as in Ezra 2 the land of Judah, now a province of the Persian kingdom; and the repetition of the verb is no contrast between city and country but a mere pleonasm of the Hebrew. What matters is the roll of classes the verse sets out, Israel, the priests, the Levites, the Nethinim, and the children of Solomon's servants, the five orders whose settlement the chapter will trace, in Jerusalem and in the towns alike.

So the witnesses hold together the moral and the documentary. Gill, Clarke, and Wesley honour the willing hearts that peopled a poor and perilous city when they might have stayed at ease in the country; Keil and Delitzsch open the ledger of the classes that follow. Between them the verse becomes both a benediction on the volunteers and the doorway into the great enrolment of the dwellers in the holy city and its villages.
3:
With the formal heading, these are the chief of the province that dwelt in Jerusalem, the register proper begins, and the witnesses at once set it beside its great parallel. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke marks a good deal of difference between this roll and the one in 1 Chronicles 9:2 and following: there, he judges, only those who came up with Zerubbabel are numbered, whereas here those first returners are joined by the people who came later with Ezra and with Nehemiah, so that the two lists, though of one city, answer to different moments of its repeopling.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott finds the very word province a fingerprint of the author. It betrays the hand of Nehemiah, he says, who was still a Persian official as well as a governor of Judah; and it shows that here we have a general heading for the whole of what follows, taking in both the city and the country named in the rest of the verse. On the word Israel he and the wesleyan-arminian John Wesley agree: it has become a generic name. The two Israelitish tribes were the bulk of the return, yet Wesley explains that the historian calls them Israel rather than Judah because many of the other tribes were now incorporated with them, and because none of the tribes save Judah and Benjamin dwelt in Jerusalem at all.

The reformed John Gill keeps to the political sense of the heading: the chief of the province means of Judea, reduced to a province by the king of Babylon and now a province of the Persian monarchy. The witnesses thus read the title on two levels at once. It is a plain administrative caption, the leading men of a Persian province settled in its chief city, and it is the seam where two sacred records meet, the Chronicler's roll of the first return and Nehemiah's fuller enrolment of the same city a lifetime later.

That doubleness governs the chapter that follows. Clarke's observation that the differences from 1 Chronicles 9 spring from the added companies of Ezra and Nehemiah, and Ellicott's that Israel now stands for the whole covenant people gathered again in Judah, prepare the reader to expect both agreement and variation as the names and numbers unfold. The heading promises a national settlement, city and country together, and the witnesses take it as Nehemiah's own summary of a people once more possessed of their land.
4:
At Jerusalem, the verse says, dwelt certain of the children of Judah and of the children of Benjamin, and the witnesses recall why both tribes met in one city. The reformed John Gill notes that Jerusalem belonged partly to the one tribe and partly to the other, and so was inhabited by both, as it had been from the first, part of the city lying in the lot of Judah and part in that of Benjamin.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch turn to the two heads of Judah's houses named here: Athaiah of the children of Perez (compare 1 Chronicles 2:4), and Maaseiah of the children of Shelah. They correct a point of the text, that the word pointed the Shilonite should be read the Shelanite, the descendants of Shelah; and they reckon the whole company of Perez at four hundred and sixty-eight able-bodied men, that is, so many fathers of families of that race, among whom the sons of Shelah, the younger brother, are probably included. Athaiah and Maaseiah themselves, they own, are not otherwise known, mere names now in a roll of the returning tribe, yet each set at the head of a house of Judah. They mark, too, a small point of the wording, that a name in the pedigree which the English keeps as an ancestor is in truth a proper name of the ordinary kind, so that the descent is drawn straight from father to father up to Perez himself, without the intrusion the unwary might suspect.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the comparison with the parallel and finds in it a small puzzle. In 1 Chronicles 9 the descendants of Perez are not given, but the descendants of Zerah, who are present there, are absent here; the two rolls of Judah's houses do not match, and this, he suggests, may be a question of the right reading of the text rather than a real difference of the families that returned. The absence of Zerah from the head of the chapter he will find the more remarkable when Zerah reappears further down among the officers.

So the witnesses read the verse as the true opening of the muster of Jerusalem's dwellers, and as the first place where its careful divergences from the Chronicler's roll come into view. Judah, the royal tribe, is named first, and named through Perez, that son of Judah of whom, as concerning the flesh, Christ came; the register begins where the promise ran, tracing the men of Judah who held the holy city, while the commentators watch, name by name, the points at which Nehemiah's copy and the older record quietly part.
5:
The second head of Judah is given with his long pedigree, Maaseiah the son of Baruch, traced back through Colhozeh, Hazaiah, Adaiah, Joiarib, and Zechariah to Shiloni, and the witnesses attend chiefly to that last name. The reformed John Gill takes this Maaseiah to be the same person elsewhere called Asaiah, and carries his descent up to Shiloni, whom he thinks perhaps the same as Shelah, another of the sons of Judah, so that the house belongs to the Shelanite branch.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott makes the point plainly: the son of Shiloni is better rendered the Shilonite, that is, of the descendants of Shelah, the youngest son of Judah; the name marks not a father called Shiloni but the clan of Shelah to which this Maaseiah belonged. So read, the two heads of Judah in the city represent the two surviving lines of the tribe that came home, the sons of Perez under Athaiah and the sons of Shelah under Maaseiah. It is a distinction easily lost, for the two names lie close in the Hebrew, and a copyist's slip or a mistaken pointing would have made the one clan vanish into a single supposed forefather; Ellicott's care recovers Shelah his rightful place in the muster.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, gathering the neighbouring verses together, count Maaseiah's house with the four hundred and sixty-eight valiant men of Perez who dwelt at Jerusalem, and then pass to the sons of Benjamin, two heads there also, Sallu at their front and, after him, Gabbai-Sallai, with nine hundred and twenty-eight fathers of families; their chief was Joel the son of Zichri, and Judah the son of Senuah was second, or prefect, over the city. Thus the two tribes are set out on the same plan, each by its leading houses, its total of able men, and its officers of the watch.

The witnesses make of this genealogical verse a lesson in the register's method rather than a story about the man, for of Maaseiah himself nothing more is known than his name and his line. What they draw out is the care with which the roll fixes each house to its father and its tribe: a single mispointed word, the Shilonite for the Shelanite, might have lost the descent of Shelah from the record, and the commentators are at pains to restore it, that both branches of Judah, the elder Perez and the younger Shelah, might stand in their places among the men who held the holy city.
6:
All the sons of Perez that dwelt at Jerusalem were four hundred threescore and eight valiant men, a bare sum, yet the witnesses find in the closing word valiant the whole point of the notice. The reformed John Gill reads it so: these four hundred and sixty-eight were valiant men, and therefore well qualified to defend the city against its enemies. In a capital newly walled and thinly peopled, the quality of its men mattered as much as their number, and the register is careful to record that the house of Judah brought not merely settlers but soldiers.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had drawn the same lesson from the muster as a whole. Though the Benjamites, he observed, were more in number, of the men of Judah it is said that they were valiant men, fit for service and able to defend the city in case of an attack; Judah has not lost its ancient character of a lion's whelp, bold and daring. The smallness of the count, a mere four hundred and sixty-eight fathers of families where the city had once teemed, he takes as a token of small beginnings, the second commonwealth rising poor and few upon the ruins of the old, yet not without the courage that its defence would need.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the reckoning, counting these four hundred and sixty-eight as the able-bodied men of the two houses of Perez and Shelah together, the fathers of families of Judah's race who settled in Jerusalem. Where the parallel record in 1 Chronicles 9 gives the men of Judah at a somewhat different tale, the commentators take the small divergence in stride, as one of the many places where Nehemiah's copy and the Chronicler's part by a handful. The number itself, they note, gathers under one head the two houses of Judah already named, Perez and Shelah alike, so that the four hundred and sixty-eight are the whole strength of the tribe within the walls, reckoned not by souls but by fathers of families able to bear arms.

The witnesses, then, make the terse verse preach the double truth of the return: a people diminished, counted now by hundreds where their fathers were counted by thousands, and yet a people not defenceless, their few made valiant, their small band of Judah fit to hold the wall. The sons of Perez, from whom the promise ran toward Christ, stand first in the muster and stand armed, the royal tribe keeping the royal city.
7:
And these are the sons of Benjamin: the register crosses from Judah to the other tribe that shared the city, and the witnesses note how evenly the two are matched. The reformed John Gill says simply that these were the men of Benjamin who inhabited Jerusalem, the house of Sallu the son of Meshullam standing at their head, with his line traced back through Joed, Pedaiah, Kolaiah, Maaseiah, and Ithiel to Jesaiah.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott draws the parallel with Judah's arrangement into a neat symmetry: the Benjamites, he observes, were represented by two families, and they gave the city two prefects, named in the verse that follows (v.9). As Judah had its two heads, Athaiah and Maaseiah, so Benjamin has its two, Sallu and, after him, Gabbai-Sallai; and as Judah's men had their overseer, so Benjamin's had their officers of the watch.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, handling the block of Benjamite verses together, set out the same order: of the Benjamites there were two heads of houses, Sallu and Gabbai-Sallai, with nine hundred and twenty-eight fathers of families; their chief was Joel the son of Zichri, and Judah the son of Senuah was second over the city. The register, they show, treats the two tribes on one plan, so that the reader may weigh house against house and number against number. The very brevity of the notice, they add, is part of its method: where the earlier verses had spread out Judah's pedigrees at length, the historian is content here to announce the tribe and pass at once to its heads and its officers, reserving his fuller words for the priests and Levites who follow.

The witnesses find in the plain formula the tribe's honour. Benjamin, the little tribe, held a share of the holy city as old as the conquest, part of Jerusalem falling within its ancient lot; and though its houses are named as briefly as Judah's, the roll gives them their full place, their leading families, their fathers of families, and their prefects. Gill's bare identification, Ellicott's symmetry of two families and two prefects, and Keil and Delitzsch's careful tally all serve the same end: to show the second commonwealth rebuilt not by one tribe only but by Judah and Benjamin together, the royal tribe and the tribe of Saul side by side within the recovered walls, each keeping its portion of the city and each answering for its defence.
8:
And after him Gabbai, Sallai, nine hundred twenty and eight: the second Benjamite house closes the tribe's tale, and the witnesses pause on the striking size of it. The reformed John Gill observes that there were more of the tribe of Benjamin in the city than of the tribe of Judah, nine hundred and twenty-eight against Judah's four hundred and sixty-eight, and offers two guesses at the reason: that Benjamin had perhaps the greater share in the city by the ancient division of the lot, or that its people were the better disposed to dwell in it.

The point is worth weighing, for it runs against the expectation. Judah was the royal and the greater tribe, yet in the holy city it was outnumbered two to one by little Benjamin. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry had marked the same fact and grounded it in the geography of the lot: though part of the city lay in Judah, the greater part was in the lot of Benjamin, and therefore here we find of Judah only four hundred and sixty-eight families, but of Benjamin nine hundred and twenty-eight. The larger number, on this reading, is no riddle of piety but the plain consequence of where the tribal boundary ran through the streets of Jerusalem.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the figure and the plan, counting the nine hundred and twenty-eight as the fathers of families of the two Benjamite houses, and then turning, with the register, to name the tribe's officers, Joel the son of Zichri their overseer, and Judah the son of Senuah second over the city. So the account of the laity is complete: two tribes, four leading houses, and their totals set down for all to see. They mark, too, that the tale of nine hundred and twenty-eight is given as the sum of both Benjamite houses together, Sallu's and Gabbai-Sallai's, so that the figure answers to the four hundred and sixty-eight of Judah's two houses, the register keeping strictly to its plan of counting each tribe by its fathers of families.

The witnesses leave the verse as a small study in the honesty of the record. It would have been easy to give Judah the pride of place in numbers as well as in rank; instead the roll reports the plain fact, that Benjamin furnished the more men, and the commentators reason soberly about it, Gill weighing affection against the accident of the lot, Henry settling it on the boundary, Keil and Delitzsch simply verifying the sum. Whether from a larger portion of the ground or a readier will, the tribe of Saul filled the greater part of the city of David, and the register honours them with the count.
9:
The Benjamites' officers are named, Joel the son of Zichri their overseer, and Judah the son of Senuah second over the city, and the witnesses divide, mildly, over what sort of office is meant. The reformed John Gill takes Joel for the chief governor of the city, the first in authority over its people. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads him likewise as chief or magistrate over the Benjamites, with Judah his second or deputy; perhaps, he allows, each had a distinct charge, but Joel's was plainly the higher.

The other wesleyan-arminian, John Wesley, gives the word a military turn: the overseer, he says, was the captain of their thousand, not a civil magistrate but the commander of the tribe's fighting men. The difference is real, if small: was Joel set over Benjamin to govern and judge, or to lead them in arms? The one reading makes him a magistrate of the peace, the other a captain of the watch; and the register, which is at once a civil roll and a muster for the wall's defence, will bear either sense.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, without settling the title, catches the reason the office is recorded at all. It is as necessary for a people to have good order kept up among themselves, he says, as to be fortified against the attacks of their enemies from abroad, to have good magistrates as to have good soldiers; and so, having told who guarded the gates, the historian is careful to tell who was overseer of the Benjamites and who was second under him. The naming of a first and a second, Henry implies, shows a settled chain of command, that the city might be well governed within as well as well defended without.

The witnesses thus turn a dry pair of names into a picture of ordered life in the restored city. Whether Joel ruled as magistrate or led as captain, and the two offices, in a frontier capital, may well have run together, the point the commentators share is that Benjamin's dwellers were not a leaderless crowd but a body under officers, a first and a second, answerable for the peace and the safety of their quarter. The register counts not only the men but the men who ordered them, and Henry's word stands over the whole: good magistrates are as needful as good soldiers. That the tribe should have both an overseer and a second, Clarke and Gill agree, argues a settled polity in the little community, not the loose gathering of a ruined people but a city taking up again the ordered government of its former days, with a chief officer and his deputy answerable for its Benjamite quarter.
10:
The register turns from the laity to the priests, and opens their roll with Jedaiah, Joiarib, and Jachin. The reformed John Gill notes that of these priests who dwelt in Jerusalem the same account is given here as in the parallel record, with one difference of name worth marking: the Seraiah named in the next verse is called Azariah in 1 Chronicles 9:11, one of the small variations that run between the two lists of the same men.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott corrects the reading of the verse itself. It should be read, he says, as three priestly families, Jedaiah, Joiarib, Jachin, set beside the same three in 1 Chronicles 9:10; the little word son that seems to make Joiarib the father of Jedaiah has, on this view, slipped into the text, where the names are in truth those of three distinct courses of the priesthood. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way, taking Jedaiah, Joiarib, and Jachin for three heads of houses, that is, of orders of priests, and judging the son before Joiarib a clerical error of the kind they had noted at the parallel place.

The witnesses thus make the priestly roll begin where the Chronicler's began, with the same three ancient courses, and they use the comparison to steady the text. Where a stray word or an altered name might mislead, Joiarib turned from a course into a father, or Azariah written for Seraiah, the commentators set the two records side by side and let each correct the other, so that the three orders stand clear.

Beneath the textual care lies the fitness of the thing. Where else, the register implies, should the priests be gathered but in the holy city, where the temple stood and their whole business lay? The men holy to God are set down first among the sacred orders that peopled Jerusalem, named by their courses as the law had ranked them, and traced through the very houses that had served before the captivity. The small divergences from 1 Chronicles 9, a name here, a word there, do not shake the substance the witnesses find in the verse: that the priesthood came home to its own city, and took up again, course by course, the ministry of the house of God. Gill's single difference of name, Seraiah for Azariah, and Ellicott's three courses in place of a father and son, are between them a fair sample of how the two records diverge, sometimes in a name, sometimes in the very grammar of the list; and the witnesses use each such difference not to discredit either roll but to read them together, confident that beneath the copyists' slips the same priesthood stands in both.
11:
Seraiah, whose pedigree is carried back through Hilkiah, Meshullam, Zadok, and Meraioth to Ahitub, is named the ruler of the house of God, and the witnesses weigh both the man and the office. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott identifies Seraiah as the high-priestly family name, the house of the chief priests, though he is careful to add that the actual occupant of the high priesthood in Nehemiah's day was Eliashib; the name here marks the line, not necessarily the living pontiff.

On the title ruler of the house of God the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke draws a sharp distinction of spheres: this ruler had the command over all the secular matters of the temple, as the high priest had over those which were spiritual. The two authorities ran side by side, the one ordering the sacred service, the other the material affairs of the house, its stores, its fabric, its provision. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set Seraiah at the head of the ministering priests and reckon their number: their brethren that did the work of the house were eight hundred and twenty-two, the body of priests belonging to the three orders here named, with Adaiah's two hundred and forty-two and Amashai's hundred and twenty-eight to follow, and Zabdiel over them all.

The reformed John Gill fixes on what the work of the house meant for those eight hundred and twenty-two: it was they who offered the sacrifices, burnt the incense, set on the shewbread, lighted the lamps, the daily round of the sanctuary, taken up again in the rebuilt temple. The largeness of the number is itself a comfort in his eyes, for so great a work required many hands, and the register shows that the labourers were not few.

The witnesses read the verse, then, as the heart of the priestly muster. Here is named the officer who governed the temple's outward estate, of the high-priestly stock; here are counted the hundreds who did its holy work. Ellicott's care to distinguish the family name from the reigning high priest, Clarke's division of the secular rule from the spiritual, and Gill's plain catalogue of the priests' daily duties together fill out a single picture: the house of God, so long desolate, now furnished again with a ruler over its affairs and an army of ministers for its altar, that the sacrifices might rise and the lamps burn as before in the recovered city.
12:
The verse repeats the tale of the ministering priests, their brethren that did the work of the house were eight hundred twenty and two, and then passes to a second priestly house, that of Adaiah the son of Jeroham, whose line is traced through Pelaliah, Amzi, Zechariah, and Pashur to Malchiah. The reformed John Gill keeps his eye on the eight hundred and twenty-two, naming again what their work was: they offered the sacrifices, burnt the incense, set on the shewbread, and lighted the lamps, the whole daily service of the house resting on their hands.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch supply the ordering that the bare numbers conceal. These eight hundred and twenty-two, they explain, belonged to the courses at whose head stood Seraiah; and Adaiah, now named, was of the house or order of Malchiah, with his own brethren, two hundred and forty-two fathers of families, to be numbered in the verse that follows. So the priesthood is set out course by course, each order with its head and its tale of men, Seraiah's, then Malchiah's, then Immer's, the whole gathered under one overseer.

The witnesses find the repetition itself instructive. That the register should twice record the eight hundred and twenty-two who did the work of the house is no mere carelessness of the copy; it marks the weight the historian lays on the fullness of the ministry. The temple's service was not a thing that a handful could maintain, the sacrifices morning and evening, the incense, the bread, the lamps, the endless round of a great sanctuary, and the roll insists, by naming the number again, that the hands were sufficient for the work.

Beneath the counting the commentators keep the dignity of the calling. To be numbered among the brethren that did the work of the house was to stand in the nearest service of God, and Adaiah's house of Malchiah, like Seraiah's before it, came home to take up that service in the rebuilt temple. The witnesses read the verse as one more course of the priesthood restored to its place, its two hundred and forty-two added to the eight hundred and twenty-two already told, that the altar of the recovered city might never want for ministers. Keil and Delitzsch's care to fix Adaiah in the order of Malchiah, and to distinguish his house from Seraiah's, shows the register doing more than heaping names; it is preserving the ancient division of the priesthood into its courses, so that a reader might know not merely how many priests came home but of which houses they were, and to which of the appointed orders each belonged.
13:
And his brethren, chief of the fathers, two hundred forty and two: the brethren of Adaiah, that is, the second order of priests. The reformed John Gill says only what the words say, that these two hundred and forty-two were the brethren, the kinsmen, of Adaiah named just before, the body of his house.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch find in the phrase a small point of grammar worth pressing. The title chief of the fathers, or heads of fathers' houses, they call striking here, for the brethren of Adaiah, being two hundred and forty-two, could not all be heads of houses but only fathers of families; the expression, strictly taken, would make each of them a chief, whereas the sense must be that they were the many fathers of families belonging to the one house whose head was Adaiah. It is a reminder that the register's honorific terms are not always to be pressed to the letter, but read as the roll's customary way of numbering a priestly course by its family men.

The witnesses keep the verse within the ordered muster of the priesthood. Adaiah's house of the order of Malchiah stands between Seraiah's course, with its eight hundred and twenty-two, and Amashai's, with its hundred and twenty-eight to come; and these two hundred and forty-two are its strength, the fathers of families who came home to serve. The number, modest beside the first course, is set down with the same care, that no order of the priesthood might be lost from the account.

Beneath the tally the commentators feel the honour of the record. To be written among the chief of the fathers of a priestly house was to hold a name in the sacred roll of those who ministered before God; and the register, keeping even the middle course of the three with its exact two hundred and forty-two, testifies that the whole priesthood, and not its greatest house only, was gathered again to the holy city. The men of Malchiah's order, obscure as their individual names now are, take their place in the muster as fathers of families sworn to the temple's service, and the historian numbers them, house by house, for the honour of their ministry and the sufficiency of the altar's servants. It is worth marking, the commentators feel, how the register weighs its words even here: the phrase chief of the fathers, which elsewhere would name the very heads of the great houses, is used of a whole company of two hundred and forty-two, so that the reader must supply the sense the roll intends and not press a title of dignity into a count of numbers.
14:
The third priestly course is described as mighty men of valour, an hundred twenty and eight, with their overseer Zabdiel, and the witnesses divide over what the valour was. The reformed John Gill and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke take it in the plain martial sense: these hundred and twenty-eight were able men to do the work of their office as priests and men of courage besides, fit to fight the enemy and defend the city upon occasion. Clarke presses the point, that they were noted for strength of body and for military courage, warriors as well as ministers, as the perilous state of the newly walled city required.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the phrase otherwise. Of valour, he says, means here able for the service of God's house, men of ability, that is, rather than men of war; the might in view is fitness for the heavy work of the sanctuary, not prowess in arms. So the same words that Gill and Clarke fill with the clash of battle, Ellicott fills with the strenuous labour of the temple, and the reader is left to weigh which the register intends, or whether, in a city that was at once a garrison and a shrine, the two ran together.

Ellicott adds a point on the overseer's name. Where the English calls Zabdiel the son of one of the great men, he would render it rather the son of Haggedolim, taking the words for a proper name; the grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch read it the same way, Zabdiel ben Haggedolim, the chief set over all the priests here numbered. The little phrase, on this reading, is not a note of the man's rank but the name of his father.

The witnesses gather the verse into the close of the priestly muster. Three courses have now been told, Seraiah's eight hundred and twenty-two, Adaiah's two hundred and forty-two, and Amashai's hundred and twenty-eight, and over them Zabdiel as overseer. Whether their valour was of the sword or of the sanctuary, the priests of the restored city are set down as strong men, equal to a service that in that day required both the offering of sacrifice and, if need be, the defence of the walls; and the register, having numbered them, turns from the priests to the Levites who served beside them. The disagreement over the valour, Gill and Clarke reading it of arms and Ellicott of ability for the sanctuary, is the more instructive because the same Hebrew word had described the fighting men of Judah a few verses before; whether the priests were valiant to defend or valiant to labour, the roll plainly means to mark them as men of strength, and the two readings only widen the sense of a priesthood equal to whatever the hour demanded.
15:
With a single phrase the register crosses from the priests to the Levites, also of the Levites, and names first Shemaiah, whose line is drawn through Hashub, Azrikam, and Hashabiah to Bunni. The reformed John Gill notes only that these were the Levites who, like the priests before them, dwelt in Jerusalem, gathered to the city where the house of God stood and their ministry lay.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, taking the Levite verses as one block, set Shemaiah of the house of Bunni at the head of the order, and unfold the three divisions into which the Levites of Jerusalem fell. There were those, like Shemaiah's house, charged with the work of the house of God; there were Shabbethai and Jozabad, of the chief of the Levites, set over the outward business of the sanctuary; and there were the singers, the sons of Asaph, whose office the register will name in its turn. The Levites, fewer than the priests, are ranked by their several charges, that each part of the service might have its ministers.

The witnesses keep before the reader why the Levites should be in the city at all, and why so few of them. Much of the Levites' proper work, as the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry elsewhere observes, was to teach the knowledge of God up and down the country, for which they were scattered through the towns of Israel; only as many as the temple required attended at Jerusalem, the rest doing good elsewhere. So the roll of Levites in the holy city is a chosen remnant, drawn in for the sanctuary's service while their brethren kept the country.

The commentators read the bare opening as the doorway into that ordered ministry. Shemaiah's house stands first, of the division that did the work of the house; behind him lie the overseers of the outward business and the singers of Asaph, each to be named as the register proceeds. The Levites, like the priests, came home course by course to the city of the temple, and the historian, faithful to his plan, sets down their heads and their charges, that the whole household of God's servants, priests, Levites, singers, and porters, might be seen restored to their places in the recovered Jerusalem. That the roll should open the Levites' account with a single house, Shemaiah's of the line of Bunni, and then unfold the rest by their offices rather than by long pedigrees, is itself of a piece with the register's method: the priests it counted by their courses, the Levites it ranks by their charges, each order set down in the way that best shows its service, so that the whole ministry of the house appears not as a crowd of names but as a body fitly ordered for its work.
16:
Two Levites, Shabbethai and Jozabad, are set over the outward business of the house of God, and the witnesses gather to explain that curious office. The reformed John Gill places them with Shemaiah among the chief of the Levites, a leading pair charged with a particular trust. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott calls the phrase a remarkable specification of the Levites' functions, set here in parallel with the valour ascribed to the priests just before; the outward business, he adds, is explained by the arrangements of the preceding chapter, where the ordering of the temple's supplies and dues was set in train.

What that business was, the witnesses fill in from several sides. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, following Calmet, takes it for the whole material provision of the sanctuary: the finding of victuals for the priests, of victims for the sacrifices, of the sacerdotal vestments and the sacred vessels, and whatever else the service required. His fellow wesleyan-arminian John Wesley looks rather to the country: the outward business, he says, concerned those things belonging to the temple and its service which were to be done without it, abroad in the land, the gathering of the voluntary contributions and other necessary provision out of the several parts of the country. The one reads the office inward, as the stewardship of the temple's stores; the other outward, as the collecting of its revenues from the villages; and between them the phrase is given its full compass, from the field where the offering was raised to the storehouse where it was kept.

Clarke marks besides a curiosity of the text, that this verse, with several others further on, is wanting in the Septuagint, and that the whole chapter is absent from the Arabic, whose translator, he supposes, had no concern with Jewish genealogies. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the office from the Hebrew, taking Shabbethai and Jozabad for two of the chief Levites set over the labour, or business, of the house of God, a charge distinct from the sacred service within, yet needful to it.

The witnesses find in the office a dignity of its own. As the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry says elsewhere of such a Levite, those who take care of the outward concerns of the church, the serving of its tables, are as necessary in their place as those who give themselves to the word and prayer; for without the secular provision the inward business of the sanctuary would be starved and stand still. So Shabbethai and Jozabad, though they handled stores and dues rather than incense and sacrifice, are honoured in the register as pillars of the restored worship, the men who kept the house supplied that the altar might never fail.
17:
Mattaniah, of the sons of Asaph, is named the principal to begin the thanksgiving in prayer, and the witnesses fix on that singular office of leading the temple's praise. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives it its plain name: Mattaniah was the precentor, the pitcher of the tune, the master-singer who set the psalm and led the rest. His fellow wesleyan-arminian John Wesley explains where and when he led, in the public and solemn prayers and praises which were constantly joined with the morning and evening sacrifice, at which the singers were present and praised God with a psalm or hymn that this man began.

The reformed John Gill adds a small point of the pedigree, that the Zabdi named in Mattaniah's line is the same person called Zichri elsewhere, one of the variant spellings that thread the register. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set Mattaniah at the head of the singers, with Bakbukiah second among his brethren, and Abda the son of Shammua, of the line of Jeduthun, beside him, the leaders of the temple's song, of the great singing houses of Asaph and Jeduthun.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the office into a lesson on worship. Thanksgiving, he observes, is necessary in prayer, and the two should go together, for giving thanks for former mercies is a becoming way of begging further mercies; and Mattaniah, chosen to begin the thanksgiving, was set to lead the congregation into that joined praise. Care should be taken in the public service, Henry adds, that everything be done decently and in good order, in prayer, that one speak and the rest join; in singing, that one begin and the rest follow, and this was Mattaniah's very charge, to begin, that the rest might come after.

The witnesses read the verse, then, as the register's tribute to the ministry of praise. Where the priests offered and the doorkeepers guarded, the singers lifted the psalm, and one man was appointed to lead them, that the worship might not fall into confusion but rise in order, one voice beginning and the choir following. Clarke's precentor, Wesley's leader of the sacrifice-praises, and Henry's reflection on thanksgiving joined to prayer converge on a single picture: the restored temple resounding again with ordered song, and Mattaniah of Asaph standing at its head to raise the note, that the house of God might be filled, as of old, with the voice of thanksgiving.
18:
All the Levites in the holy city were two hundred fourscore and four: the register sums the order it has been numbering, and the witnesses pause on both the total and the title. The reformed John Gill notes simply that these two hundred and eighty-four were the Levites who had their residence there, in the city itself, as distinct from their brethren scattered through the country towns.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch confirm the reckoning, taking the two hundred and eighty-four for the whole body of Levites in Jerusalem, those of Shemaiah's division over the work of the house, Shabbethai and Jozabad over the outward business, and the singers of Asaph under Mattaniah, and then passing to the porters, a hundred and seventy-two, who kept the gates. The Levites, they show, were far fewer than the priests, whose three courses alone had numbered near twelve hundred; the ministering tribe came home thin.

The witnesses feel the smallness of the number and read it as the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry read it, against the wider work of the Levites. Some of the Levites, he observes, came and dwelt at Jerusalem, yet but few in comparison, because much of their work was to teach the good knowledge of God up and down the country, for which they were to be scattered in Israel; as many as there was occasion for attended at Jerusalem, and the rest were doing good elsewhere. The two hundred and eighty-four are therefore not the whole of the order but the portion the temple required, drawn in to serve the sanctuary while their fellows kept the villages.

The title, too, the commentators do not pass over. The register calls Jerusalem the holy city, as it does at the chapter's opening, and the phrase gives the dry count its weight: these Levites dwelt where God had put his name, in the city set apart to him. It was fitting, the witnesses feel, that the ministers of holy things should have their residence in the holy city; and though they were few, their being gathered there, counted to the man, two hundred and eighty-four, is the sign that the worship of God was manned again in its proper place, the Levites restored to the sanctuary they had served before the captivity, that the house might not want for its ministers nor the holy city for its holy men. Keil and Delitzsch's reminder that these two hundred and eighty-four fell into three divisions, over the work of the house, the outward business, and the song, keeps the bare total from being a mere figure; it is the sum of a whole ordered ministry, and the smallness of it beside the priests' near twelve hundred only sharpens the sense of a tribe that came home a remnant, gathering to the temple as many as its service required and no more.
19:
The porters are numbered, Akkub, Talmon, and their brethren that kept the gates, were an hundred seventy and two, and the witnesses use the count to weigh once more against the Chronicler's roll. The reformed John Gill sets down the figure and the office plainly: a hundred and seventy-two doorkeepers, under Akkub and Talmon, whose charge was to keep the gates of the temple.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott marks a divergence here from the parallel. In 1 Chronicles 9 the porters number two hundred and twelve, where this register gives a hundred and seventy-two; and the difference between the two accounts, he suggests, may be partly explained by the fact that in the Chronicles the list is confined to those who came up with Zerubbabel, while here an addition is made of those who came later with Ezra. Yet he does not force the reconciliation, referring the reader to his fuller comment on 1 Chronicles 9, and leaving the two figures side by side as one more of the honest variations that run between the rolls.

The witnesses take the doorkeepers' office more seriously than its small number might suggest. The keeping of the gates was an ancient and sacred trust, the porters set to guard the entrances of the house of God against whatever was unclean or unfit; and the register honours them with the same care it gives the priests and singers, naming their chiefs and telling their tale. That they were but a hundred and seventy-two, where a great temple might have used more, is of a piece with the whole picture of the return, a poor and diminished people, manning the sanctuary as fully as their numbers allowed.

The divergence from 1 Chronicles 9 the commentators handle as they have handled the rest: not as a flaw to be hidden nor a contradiction to be feared, but as the natural mark of two records taken at two moments, the one of the first return under Zerubbabel, the other of the fuller city that Ezra and Nehemiah had further peopled. The forty porters by which the accounts differ are, on Ellicott's reading, simply the doorkeepers who came up in the later companies; and the register, adding them in, gives the truer count of the gate-keepers who warded the temple in Nehemiah's day. The witnesses will not let so slight a difference, forty souls in a body of some two hundred, be turned into a stumbling-block; it is precisely the kind of variation a living record gathers as it is copied and enlarged, and its presence, far from discrediting the roll, is a mark that the historian set down what he found and added what he knew, rather than smoothing the two accounts into a false agreement.
20:
And the residue of Israel, of the priests and the Levites, were in all the cities of Judah, every one in his inheritance: the register lifts its eye from the capital to the country, and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry takes the verse as the hinge of the whole account. Having named the chief persons who dwelt in Jerusalem, Nehemiah now turns to the other cities in which dwelt the residue of Israel; for it was requisite that Jerusalem should be replenished, yet not so as to drain the country. The king himself, Henry says, is served of the field, which will do little service if there be not hands to manage it; let there therefore be no strife, no envy, no contempt, between the inhabitants of the cities and those of the villages, for both are needful, both useful, and neither can be spared.

The reformed John Gill states the plain sense, that these were all the priests and Levites besides those settled at Jerusalem, dispersed through the towns of Judah, every one in his own inheritance. Upon that frame Henry hangs the details the following verses will give. The Nethinim, the posterity of the Gibeonites, dwelt in Ophel, hard by the temple whose servile work they did; the Levites, though scattered through the cities, had an overseer resident in Jerusalem to whom they looked; some of the singers were set over the repairs and business of the house of God, and the king of Persia allowed them a maintenance; and one of the seed of Zerah was the king's commissioner at Jerusalem, of that family of Judah of which some were now new-settled in the city, though the older catalogue in 1 Chronicles 9:6 had named the sons of Pharez there.

Henry then reads the country settlement with a prophet's shadow over it. Here follow, he says, the villages inhabited by the residue of Israel, the towns of Judah, the towns of Benjamin, and the divisions of the Levites among both; and we may now suppose them safe and easy, though few and poor. By the blessing of God they were likely to increase in wealth and power, and would have increased the more, he laments, had there not been that general profaneness and lukewarmness in religion with which the prophet Malachi, who lived about this time, charged them in God's name, Malachi, in whom prophecy ceased for some ages, till it revived in the great prophet and his forerunner.

The witnesses thus make the verse the seam between city and country in the restored nation. Gill fixes the plain fact of the dispersal; Henry draws out its wisdom, that a capital must be filled without emptying the fields, and its danger, that a people spared and settled may yet be undone by their own coldness toward God. The residue of Israel, priests and Levites and laity alike, are set down each in his inheritance, a whole people repossessed of their land, and the historian, with the villages still to name, pauses to remind the reader that city and country were one body.
21:
The lowest of the temple's servants are placed apart, the Nethinims dwelt in Ophel, and Ziha and Gispa were over the Nethinims, and the witnesses agree on the fitness of their station. The reformed John Gill takes Ophel for a high place or tower upon the wall of Jerusalem, where these given ones had their quarter. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley explains why they were lodged just there: the Nethinim dwelt in Ophel, which was upon the wall of the city, because they were to do the servile work of the temple, and so were to be posted near it, that they might be ready to attend.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the place more exactly as the southern slope of Mount Moriah, the ridge running down from the temple hill, the same Ophel named earlier in the book (Nehemiah 3:26). Their chiefs, they add, were Zihah and Gispa; and they note that a Ziha stands at the head of a division of Nethinim in Ezra 2:43, though they decline the attempt of Bertheau to identify Gispa with a name that follows there, judging the likeness too slight to build upon. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds a nicety of the ground: the Nethinim on the promontory of Ophel were either within or without the city, according as the one wall or the other was reckoned the boundary, and here, he judges, they are regarded as outside.

The witnesses read the verse as a picture of humble service honoured with a place. The Nethinim were the descendants of the Gibeonites, given of old to the meanest offices of the sanctuary, the drawers of water and hewers of wood; and here they are lodged on the slope beneath the temple, near enough to be always at hand for its drudgery. That the register should name their very dwelling and their two chiefs, Ziha and Gispa, is of a piece with the honour it pays every order of the Lord's house, down to the lowest.

So the commentators leave the given ones in their proper station, on the ridge of Ophel below the courts they served. Gill's tower on the wall, Wesley's reason of nearness, Keil and Delitzsch's slope of Moriah, and Ellicott's question of the boundary all serve the one sense: that even the temple-bondsmen had their appointed place in the restored city, close under the sanctuary whose servile work was theirs, numbered and named in the roll of a people come home.
22:
Over the Levites of Jerusalem is set an overseer, Uzzi the son of Bani, and the witnesses attend both to his office and to his descent. The reformed John Gill calls him the supervisor of the Levites, who looked after them that they did their work in ministering to the priests as there was occasion; and he traces the man's line through Hashabiah and Mattaniah up to Micha the son of Asaph, so binding the overseer to the great singing house.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke lingers on the title. The word rendered overseer is the visitant or inspector, the officer who went among the Levites to see their duty done; and he notes that both the Septuagint and the Vulgate rendered it bishop, the very word that would later name the overseers of the church. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott agrees on the sense, a visitor, and would read the whole of Uzzi's pedigree together, the son of Micha, of the sons of Asaph, the singers in the service of the house of God, so that Uzzi appears as chief of the Levites precisely in his character as one of the singing line, a parallel, he notes, to the leader of thanksgiving named in v.17.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch make the verse a supplement to an earlier one. The business of the house of God over which Uzzi presided was, they explain, the very duty assigned to the Levites of Shemaiah's house at v.15, whose chiefs had not there been named; the register now supplies the omission, naming Uzzi, of the sons of Asaph, as their head. So the three divisions of the Levites each have their president told, those over the outward business, the singers, and now those over the work of the house.

The witnesses find in the office the same care for order that marks the whole muster. It was not enough that the Levites be gathered and numbered; they must be overseen, that their ministry be duly performed, and so a visitor is set over them, resident in the city, of the honoured stock of Asaph. Clarke's bishop, Ellicott's singer-overseer, and Keil and Delitzsch's supplement to the roll of Shemaiah all draw one figure: Uzzi, inspector of the Levites of the holy city, keeping his brethren to their charge, that the service of the house of God might go forward without fault in the recovered temple.
23:
For it was the king's commandment concerning them, that a certain portion should be for the singers, due for every day, and the witnesses divide over which king is meant. The reformed John Gill leaves the question open, allowing that some understand it of King David, who first ordered the courses of the singers, and others of the king of Persia then reigning. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke weighs the same two and comes down for the Persian: it is most probable, he says, that the king was Artaxerxes, who wished a provision made for these singers, part of whose office was to offer up prayers as well as praises. He supports it from precedent, that Darius had made ample provision for the priests, that they might offer sacrifices of sweet savour to the God of heaven and pray for the life of the king and his sons (Ezra 6:10), and even conjectures that these had been Jewish singers employed in the Persian king's own service, to whom he wished to continue their salary.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads it the same way and makes the grant precise: Artaxerxes had gone beyond the mere exemption from tribute allowed the temple-servants in Ezra 7:24, and had given the singers a daily allowance, which it was the business of Uzzi the overseer to see paid. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch likewise take the commandment for a royal ordinance settling a fixed daily portion on the singers, part of the same care of the Persian court for the worship at Jerusalem that runs through these books.

So the debate stands between David, the founder of the temple's music, and Artaxerxes, its foreign patron, the one a plausible source for the order of the singers, the other for a daily maintenance paid out of the province. The weight of the witnesses falls on the Persian king, and Gill alone keeps the older name in play.

Yet the commentators agree on what the verse discloses, whichever king gave the word: that the singers of the restored temple did not serve at their own charge, but had a settled provision, day by day, secured to them by royal command. The mercy of it, Clarke feels, is that a heathen monarch should so care for the praises of the God of Israel as to fund them from his treasury; and the register, in noting the daily portion, shows the worship of the recovered house resting not only on the freewill of the people but on a maintenance the empire itself had guaranteed, that the song might never fail for want of bread.
24:
Pethahiah the son of Meshezabeel, of the children of Zerah the son of Judah, is named as the man who was at the king's hand in all matters concerning the people, and the witnesses describe both his lineage and his office. The reformed John Gill notes his descent from Zerah, the twin brother of Pharez, so that this officer sprang from the second of Judah's twin sons, the line not commonly followed in the register.

That descent gives the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott a textual puzzle. Pethahiah's being of the children of Zerah, he observes, makes the absence of Zerah at the beginning of the chapter very remarkable, and suggests some accidental omission in the roll of Judah's houses, where Perez was named but Zerah was not; the officer at the chapter's close belongs to a family the muster at its head had passed over. On the office itself Ellicott is plain: Pethahiah was the king's agent in all the country matters of the province, the man through whom the affairs of the whole Jewish community were transacted at the Persian court.

The wesleyan-arminian witnesses fill in his work. Adam Clarke makes him the governor appointed by the Persian king over the Jewish nation in those matters where the civil government touched their concerns, and doubts not that he fixed, levied, and received the tribute. John Wesley reads the phrase at the king's hand as meaning on the king's part, set to determine civil causes and controversies between man and man by the laws of that kingdom, and between the king and the people, as in matters of tribute or of grievances. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch agree that he stood at the king's hand, transacting the business of the community at the royal court rather than as a mere commissioner resident in Jerusalem.

The witnesses read the verse as the meeting-point of the two authorities under which the restored nation lived. Pethahiah was a Jew, of the seed of Judah through Zerah, yet he served as the empire's officer, the channel between the people and their Persian lord in all that concerned tribute and justice; and it was a happy thing, the commentators feel, that one of themselves should hold so sensitive a post. The register, having numbered priests and Levites and given ones, closes its account of the men of place with this officer of the crown, and Ellicott's note on the missing Zerah reminds the reader that even here, near the end, the roll invites comparison with itself, its officer sprung from a house its opening had somehow let fall.
25:
With the men of place all named, the register turns to the country towns, for the villages, with their fields, some of the children of Judah dwelt at Kirjath-arba, and at Dibon, and at Jekabzeel, and the witnesses take up the geography of the settlement. The reformed John Gill marks the change of subject: the account now passes from Jerusalem to the cities and villages of the country, and to the inhabitants of them.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch handle the wording with their usual care. They render the opening with respect to the towns in their fields, noting the peculiar introductory particle that governs the list; the word for villages, they explain, means properly enclosures, the unwalled towns and boroughs of Leviticus 25:31, while the fields are the field-boundaries about them, and the daughters of a town are the hamlets and estates that belonged to it, as so often in the town-lists of Joshua. The places themselves they fix: Kirjath-arba is Hebron (Genesis 23:2), and Jekabzeel is the Kabzeel of the old inheritance (Joshua 15:21).

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads the verse as a general notice of how the children of Judah were now distributed, and dwells on the recovered name of Hebron. Kirjath-arba, he observes, is Hebron no longer called by its later name but by the ancient one, restored to the old town on the people's return; and he marks the point of vocabulary Keil and Delitzsch also made, that the villages thereof is literally the daughters thereof, a different word from the villages at the head of the verse.

The witnesses find in the list the completion of the whole design. The register had peopled the holy city; now it shows the residue of Judah spread through their ancient towns, Hebron and Dibon and Jekabzeel and the rest, each with its fields and its daughter-hamlets about it. The care over the words, the enclosures without walls, the daughters of the towns, is of a piece with the care over the names: the historian is not merely listing places but showing a people repossessed of their inheritance, dwelling again in the very towns their fathers had held. That the oldest name of all, Kirjath-arba, comes back to Hebron on the return is itself a small sign the commentators relish, the ancient landscape of Judah waking again to its ancient names as the exiles came home to their fields.
26:
The roll of Judah's country towns runs on, Jeshua, Moladah, Beth-phelet, Hazar-shual, Beersheba and its villages, Ziklag, Mekonah, En-rimmon, Zareah, Jarmuth, and the rest, and the witnesses read it as the mapping of a people spread again through the southland. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch gather the whole stretch together, following the towns down through Zanoah and Adullam to Lachish with its fields and Azekah with its villages, and marking the summary that closes the list: the children of Judah dwelt from Beersheba unto the valley of Hinnom, the one at the far south, the other at the very edge of Jerusalem.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke pauses on the first name in the list, Jeshua, only to own the limit of knowledge: this city, he says, is nowhere else mentioned in Scripture, a town whose very site is lost, known now by this single notice in the register of the return. It is a small confession that runs through the whole catalogue, that of many of these places nothing survives but the bare name, set down here because Judah's people once more dwelt there.

The witnesses take the list, for all its obscurity, as a true record of the inheritance repossessed. These were the towns of the south, the Negeb of Judah, Beersheba the old well of the patriarchs, Ziklag that had been David's refuge, Adullam of his cave, Lachish the fenced city, and the return set families in them again, from the desert border in the south to the ravine below the holy city in the north. The register does not linger over their histories; it counts them home.

So the commentators read the verse as one more panel of the settlement. Keil and Delitzsch trace the line of towns across the land, Clarke marks how far the ancient geography has faded, and both leave the plain sense standing: that the children of Judah, having filled their share of Jerusalem, spread out to hold their old towns and fields once more. The register does not tell how many dwelt in each place, as it had counted the houses of the city; it is content to name the towns, and to let the long file of them, Jeshua and Moladah and Beth-phelet and Hazar-shual and all the rest, stand as the roll of a countryside repossessed. The naming of Beersheba and the valley of Hinnom as the bounds of their dwelling gives the measure of it, the whole breadth of Judah, from the wilderness to the walls, peopled again by the men who had come up from the captivity to their own cities.
30:
The catalogue of Judah's towns ends where the verse names its last places, Zanoah, Adullam, Lachish with its fields, Azekah with its villages, and rounds off with the reach of the whole: they dwelt from Beersheba unto the valley of Hinnom. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott seizes on that closing measure. The men of Judah, he observes, spread from the extreme south to the extreme north of Judah, an extent of some fifty miles, from Beersheba on the desert border to the valley of Hinnom under the wall of Jerusalem, the length of the tribe's inheritance filled again with its people.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch, closing their survey of the southern towns, mark the same bound: Beersheba at the one end, the valley of Hinnom at the other, the two named to set the compass of Judah's resettlement. Between them lie the towns the verse has just told, Adullam of the cave, Lachish the fortress, Azekah of the valley, each with its fields and daughter-hamlets, the old strongholds of the south inhabited once more.

The witnesses find in that single phrase, from Beersheba unto the valley of Hinnom, the whole point of the country-list. It is not a random scatter of villages but a measured possession, stretching the length of Judah, so that a reader may see at a glance how far the returning tribe had spread. Fifty miles of hill and lowland, from the wilderness well where Abraham and Isaac had dug and sworn, to the ravine at the very gate of the holy city, were peopled again by the children of the captivity.

So the commentators read the closing notice as a quiet triumph of the register. The exile had emptied the land; the return has filled it, corner to corner, from the southern desert to the northern capital. Ellicott's fifty miles and Keil and Delitzsch's two boundary-marks together give the settlement its shape, a whole province repossessed, its ancient towns awake again, the men of Judah dwelling from end to end of the inheritance their fathers had lost and God had given back. The dry list of names, sealed with this measure of its breadth, becomes the record of a people once more at home in all their borders. Ellicott's plain arithmetic of fifty miles, the witnesses feel, does more than fix a distance; it lets the reader see the shape of the mercy, a tribe that had been carried captive to a far land now stretched again from its southern well to its northern ravine, holding the length of its inheritance as fully as in the days before the exile, and holding it by the appointment of the same God who had once given it and had now restored it.
31:
The register crosses to the other tribe of the settlement, the children of Benjamin from Geba dwelt at Michmash, and Aija, and Bethel, and the witnesses map the Benjamite towns north of the capital. The reformed John Gill sets the compass first: Geba was a city on the southern border of Benjamin and Michmash on the northern, so that the tribe's dwellings ran the breadth of its land. He runs down the names that follow, Aija, the same as the Ai that lay east of Bethel; Anathoth, the birthplace of the prophet Jeremiah; Nob, the city of the priests; Ananiah, Hazor, to be distinguished from the Hazor of Naphtali; Ramah, Gittaim, Hadid, Zeboim, Neballat, Lod, and Ono, with the valley of craftsmen at the last.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott corrects the phrasing of the opening: from Geba should be read as the children of Benjamin dwelt from Geba to Michmash, the two towns marking the ends of their range as Beersheba and Hinnom had marked Judah's. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch fix the sites on the ground, Geba, the old northern boundary of the kingdom of Judah (2 Kings 23:8), a half-ruined village some three leagues north of Jerusalem; Michmash, now Mukhmas, north-east of it; and Aija, the Aiath of the prophet's march (Isaiah 10:28), so that the reader may follow the settlement town by town over the hills of Benjamin.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds a single identification, that Geba is probably the same as Gibeah of Saul, the seat of Israel's first king; the tribe of Benjamin dwelt again about the very town from which its greatest son had reigned.

The witnesses read the verse, then, as the northern counterpart to Judah's southern list. Where Judah spread from Beersheba to Hinnom, Benjamin spread from Geba to Michmash and beyond, filling its own hill-country with the returned families and reclaiming names heavy with the sacred story, Ai of Joshua's battle, Anathoth of Jeremiah, Nob of the slaughtered priests, Gibeah of Saul. The commentators do not moralize the list; they locate it, Gill running through the towns, Ellicott mending the phrase, Keil and Delitzsch pinning the sites, Clarke recalling the king's city. Between them they show the little tribe repossessed of its ancient ground, its villages awake again north of Jerusalem, so that both tribes of the settlement, Judah and Benjamin, are seen dwelling from border to border of their inheritance.
32:
The Benjamite towns continue, and at Anathoth, Nob, Ananiah, and the witnesses, having mapped the tribe's borders, dwell on the memories these names carry. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch take the verse with those around it as the roll of the villages inhabited by Benjamin, following the line through Anathoth and Nob and Ananiah to Hazor and Ramah and the rest, the towns of the tribe's hill-country resettled by the returned families.

The reformed John Gill had already fixed the chief of them. Anathoth was the birthplace of the prophet Jeremiah, a priestly town of Benjamin; Nob was the city of the priests, where the tabernacle once stood and where Saul had slain the house of Ahimelech; and Ananiah, he owns, is a place nowhere else mentioned in Scripture, known only by this notice. The names range from the famous to the wholly obscure, yet all are set down alike, because Benjamin dwelt in them again.

The witnesses find the resettlement of these towns quietly weighty. Anathoth, to which Jeremiah had bidden his kinsman buy a field as a pledge that houses and fields should yet be possessed again in the land, was now in truth possessed again; the priestly Nob, whose slaughter had been one of the darkest deeds of Saul's reign, was peopled once more; and even the nameless Ananiah, of which nothing else is told, had its returned inhabitants. The register keeps the great name and the small with equal care.

So the commentators read the verse as one more stretch of the Benjamite settlement, rich in old associations but plainly recorded. Keil and Delitzsch trace the towns in order; Gill supplies their histories where any survive and confesses ignorance where none does. Between them they show the tribe of Benjamin repossessed of its sacred ground, the prophet's town, the priests' city, and the village without a story, each named in the roll of the return, that the reader might see the promise made good that the towns of Judah and Benjamin should be inhabited again, from the greatest of them to the least. There is a quiet fitness, the witnesses feel, in setting Anathoth at the head of these Benjamite names, for it was Jeremiah's own town, from a priest of Anathoth that the word had come foretelling both the captivity and the return; and now the register records that very town peopled again, the prophecy of desolation and of homecoming alike fulfilled in the place where the prophet was born. So the roll, which seems only to list villages, is found to be the visible answer to the promises spoken over them.
33:
Hazor, Ramah, Gittaim, Hadid, Zeboim, Neballat: the roll of Benjamin's towns runs on into places of which almost nothing is known, and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke owns it plainly. Hadid, he says, is a place unknown; and Neballat, likewise, is unknown, towns named here and scarcely anywhere else, their sites long since lost.

The reformed John Gill had ventured what little could be said. Hadid he took for the same as Adida, a town that lay in the plain and was afterward fortified; Zeboim he connected with a valley of that name known from the earlier history; and Neballat, he too confessed, is read of nowhere else in Scripture. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch simply set these names in their place in the list of Benjamite towns, following Hadid and Zeboim and Neballat on toward Lod and Ono at the close, without pretending to fix what cannot be fixed.

The witnesses make no more of these obscure names than the record allows, and their restraint is itself instructive. Where a place can be identified, the commentators identify it; where, as here, the town has vanished from all other memory, they say so and pass on. The register is not diminished by the obscurity: that Hadid and Neballat cannot now be found on any map does not unmake the fact that families of Benjamin dwelt in them on the return, and were counted there by the historian.

So the verse stands as a lesson in the honesty of the catalogue. It would have been easy to name only the famous towns and let the rest fall away; instead the roll keeps the unknown places beside the known, Hadid and Zeboim and Neballat between the priestly Nob and the well-attested Lod. The commentators, unable to tell their stories, will not invent them, but neither will they drop them; they leave the obscure villages in the record where the return set their inhabitants, a token that God's account of his repossessing people overlooked no town, however small or however soon forgotten, in which they came again to dwell. Gill's ventured guesses, that Hadid was the later Adida of the plain and Zeboim a valley known of old, show the commentators reaching for what light the rest of Scripture affords; and where even that fails, as with Neballat, they are content to confess ignorance rather than invent, letting the bare name stand as the sole surviving trace of a Benjamite village that once held its returned families and is now known by this notice alone.
35:
The Benjamite list closes with Lod, and Ono, the valley of craftsmen, and the witnesses find in these last names a little more foothold than in the towns just before. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke traces Lod and Ono to their builders: these towns, he says, were built by the sons of Elpaal, as the genealogy of Benjamin records (1 Chronicles 8:12); and the valley of craftsmen he connects with the notice in 1 Chronicles 4:14, judging that a town of that name was probably built in the valley by the artisans from whom it took its title.

The reformed John Gill had set Lod and Ono among the towns of Benjamin, and named the valley of craftsmen, the Ge-harashim of the older record, as the place of the workers in wood and metal. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch close their survey of the villages with these same three names, Lod, Ono, and the valley of craftsmen, the last stretch of Benjamin's resettlement on the western edge of its land, toward the plain.

The witnesses take the naming of the craftsmen's valley as a homely touch fitting the whole account. Where the register had counted priests and Levites and singers for the sanctuary, it counts here a valley of artisans, the smiths and carpenters whose trade would be needed to rebuild a ruined land; the returning people brought back not only their worshippers but their workmen, and a whole vale was known for their craft. That its town was built, as Clarke supposes, by the artificers themselves gives the place a plain dignity, a settlement raised by the hands that worked in it.

So the commentators bring the catalogue of Benjamin's towns to its end. Lod and Ono, ascribed to the old builders of Elpaal's line, and the valley of craftsmen, named for its trades, complete the roll of the tribe's dwellings from Geba in the east to the lowland in the west. The register, having peopled the holy city, the towns of Judah, and now the towns of Benjamin down to this valley of workmen, has traced the whole settlement of the returned nation; and the witnesses, fixing these last names by the parallels in Chronicles, leave the account ready for its closing word on the Levites dispersed among both tribes. That the two towns should be tied to the sons of Elpaal, and the valley to its craftsmen, gives the commentators a rare foothold in a stretch of otherwise obscure names; and the homely detail, a vale named for its smiths and carpenters, reminds them that a nation resettling a ruined land had need of hands skilled in wood and iron no less than of priests and singers, so that even the trades of the people find their quiet place in the sacred roll of the return.
36:
The chapter ends with a brief word on the Levites, and of the Levites were divisions in Judah, and in Benjamin, and the witnesses read it as the fitting close of the whole settlement. The reformed John Gill takes it to mean that the Levites were scattered about, some here and some there, in both these tribes, for the better instruction of the people; dispersed among the towns, they were within reach of all, to teach the knowledge of God through the land.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads the sense the same way, that the Levites had their dwellings in the divisions of Judah and Benjamin, and rejects a rendering he thinks unlikely, the Syriac's, that they had the half of Judah and Benjamin. He adds a sober reflection on their maintenance: the people, whose hearts were now turned toward the Lord, would surely make the best provision they could for the support of God's work and all engaged in it; yet it could not be great, for the complete service was not yet established, and the Levites themselves were few in number.

The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the wording and the reason. Keil and Delitzsch render the clause to mean that divisions of Levites who by former arrangement had belonged to Judah now came to Benjamin, and dwelt among the Benjamites, the ministering families redistributed as the resettlement required. Charles Ellicott adds why the notice is so brief: the fewness of the Levites in the country warranted their summary mention in this way, a whole order dismissed in a line because there were now so few of them to record.

The witnesses gather the verse, and with it the chapter, into a single sense. The great muster that began with the casting of lots to bring one in ten into the holy city ends with the Levites spread thin through the towns of both tribes, that no part of the land might be without its teachers of the law. Gill's scattering for instruction, Clarke's care for their support, Keil and Delitzsch's redistribution, and Ellicott's note on their fewness all serve the one picture: a restored people settled city and country alike, and their ministers dispersed among them, few but faithful, that the knowledge of God might go with the nation into every town it had reclaimed. So the register closes, not with a number but with the Levites at their work in the midst of the people, the last of the orders to be set in its place in the recovered land.
